strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation problem for brain-to-text generation: distinguishing performance on familiar subjects or stimuli from generalization to unseen subjects and unseen language. A reliable benchmark for the latter would be valuable to NLP research.

The intended requirement of disjoint subjects and stimuli is appropriate for the stated generalization target. Recognizing that overlapping fMRI windows require additional care beyond splitting complete EEG examples is a useful methodological distinction.

The experiments cover two public datasets, two established decoding architectures, and several splitting strategies. Four-seed overlap diagnostics and training-duration comparisons provide useful breadth, while Appendix A supplies some training and preprocessing details.
weaknesses: The published algorithms do not enforce the central guarantee. Algorithm 1, line 15, checks the subject assignment but not the text assignment, so it can add an edge connecting a training subject to a test text. Algorithm 2, line 33, checks the task assignment but not the subject assignment, allowing test-subject data into training. Both endpoints must belong to the destination partition. These are substantive contradictions between the pseudocode and the claimed absence of leakage.

The leakage metrics are inconsistent with their stated interpretation. Equation 8 counts exact signal intersections, whereas the paper defines brain-signal leakage as any recordings from a shared subject. Disjoint recordings from the same subject therefore need not produce a nonzero intersection. Its denominator is also zero for entirely held-out subjects, without a defined convention. Consequently, Table 1 cannot be reliably reconstructed from the equations.

Several ROUGE results require correction or explanation. In Table 4, EEG2Text has recall 23.98, precision 23.95, and F-score 25.74; Table 3 contains similar cases. F1 cannot exceed both precision and recall under standard, consistently aggregated ROUGE scoring. The metric implementation and aggregation must be audited before the benchmark results can be trusted.

The experiments do not establish the claimed causal effects of leakage. Improving validation loss or generation scores over additional epochs is not itself evidence of memorization or encoder degradation. Splitting changes subject familiarity, stimulus familiarity, and potentially retained training size; Table 2 additionally changes initialization, learning rate, and training duration. Matched comparisons and language-only or shuffled-signal controls are needed to support claims that the decoder memorizes text and the encoder contributes little.

The claim that all existing splitting methods suffer from leakage conflates different evaluation targets. Holding out stories while retaining subjects can legitimately evaluate new-language decoding for known users; holding out subjects with shared stimuli evaluates another form of transfer. These protocols do not establish simultaneous generalization along both axes, but that does not automatically make them invalid. The criticism should distinguish actual sample contamination from a mismatch between a protocol and its claimed generalization target.

Reproducibility remains insufficient for the proposed benchmark. The manuscript supplies no release link or exact split manifests, and does not clearly specify the test-time decoding protocol, including whether ground-truth prefixes are supplied. Model scores lack uncertainty across subject partitions and training seeds; the four seeds reported in Table 1 concern overlap diagnostics only. This matters particularly for ZuCo's small participant pool.

The claimed gains in data utilization and model generalization are not demonstrated. Retained and discarded sample counts, achieved partition sizes, and comparisons with simpler valid splitting procedures are missing. A stricter evaluation protocol measures generalization but does not itself show that models generalize better. Correcting the algorithms and metrics, releasing reproducible splits, and adding controlled validation are necessary before a sound Findings recommendation.
